chapter: Young players, schools and studio work
title: Defending Louis Armstrong against the Uncle Tom charge
summary: Maxwell says Armstrong slipped dignity into his records and needs no apology, and notes Clark Terry, Dizzy and Royal know his playing.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: You know, there's some talk in some circles, him being an Uncle Tom, from people who have no relativity with the era in which Louis lived. And how he had to survive.

Well, he survived. And if it wasn't for him, you wouldn't have the young people today who are in a position where they can call him an Uncle Tom, and get away with it. He made his little remarks. You know that yourself, like he'd make his little digs on records, like "Just a Gigolo," he slips in, "when I die I know they'll say, just another jig." And here and there, "shine," "chocolate drop, that's me" and sang it with great feeling. And although, "Black and Blue," "What did I do to be so black and blue," wasn't his song, and he didn't change the words, he sang it with sincerity. I think there was no mistaking that song was written for him. And it could make a white person feel black when you'd hear it, if it's possible. I could have cried right along with him when he did that record.
I know, I've felt that same thing.

So I don't think he has to apologize to anybody or anybody has to apologize for him. It's shocking that a lot of people who said that were musicians themselves, and were angry young musicians at the time. But you know, going back to black musicians doing it, you take guys like

Clark Terry, Dizzy Gillespie, Ernie Royal, who were older than those other two, they know a lot of Louis's stuff, much to my surprise. And they're considerably younger, you know. They weren't learning at the time that Louis was at his peak. Well, Dizzy is not ten or fifteen years younger, he's the same age as me. But Clark is younger and a lot of good musicians know it.
